title: 5-4-3-2-1 grounding technique
content: When anxious thoughts start spiraling, grounding techniques can help bring attention back to the present moment. One simple method: name 5 things you can see around you, 4 things you can touch, 3 things you can hear, 2 things you can smell, and 1 thing you can taste. This works by shifting mental focus away from anxious 'what if' thoughts and toward concrete sensory details, which can interrupt the spiral and create a small sense of steadiness.

title: Box breathing for physical anxiety symptoms
content: Anxiety often shows up physically first - racing heart, shallow breathing, tight chest. Box breathing can help regulate this: breathe in slowly for 4 counts, hold for 4 counts, breathe out for 4 counts, hold for 4 counts, then repeat. Doing this for even one or two minutes can slow a racing heart rate and signal to the nervous system that it's safe to calm down. It's discreet enough to do anywhere, including in the middle of a stressful situation.

title: Scheduling a 'worry window'
content: Constant anxious thoughts throughout the day can feel exhausting and hard to control. One approach some people find helpful is setting aside a specific 10-15 minute 'worry window' each day - when anxious thoughts pop up outside that window, jot them down briefly and consciously postpone thinking about them until the scheduled time. This doesn't make worries disappear, but it can reduce how much they interrupt daily life, and often by the time the worry window arrives, some of the thoughts feel less urgent.

title: When anxiety may need professional support
content: Occasional anxiety is a normal part of life, but it may be worth speaking with a doctor or therapist if anxious feelings are persistent (most days for weeks), interfere with sleep, work, or relationships, or come with physical symptoms like a racing heart or panic attacks that happen often. A professional can help identify whether this is generalized anxiety, panic disorder, or something else, and explore options like therapy (CBT is particularly well-studied for anxiety) or, if appropriate, medication.
